episode_title: Nothing is Indian! Everything is Indian!

stories.summary: Salmon sushi did not exist until the 1980s. Norway was harvesting more salmon than it could store and needed export markets, so it sent Bjorn Erik Olsen to Japan. The Japanese objected that the salmon was too pink and not red enough, and local salmon was associated with parasites. An advertising campaign about Norway's pure waters failed. As a last resort, Olsen offered the food company Nichirei thousands of tons of salmon at a very cheap price on the condition that it be sold as sushi. It took off. Amit says this was the point at which sushi became a global dish, because mild salmon sushi suited Western palates. Ramen, he adds, is also relatively recent.
stories.insight: Dishes that feel ancient and authentic are often recent accidents of trade. Here a Norwegian storage problem ended up popularising Japanese food around the world.
stories.quote: But the truth is that salmon sushi as a concept did not exist till the nineteen eighties.

stories.summary: Ajay starts from James C. Scott: grain is calorie-dense, storable, transportable and easy to seize, so armies roaming Europe's wars stripped villages of it. The young Frederick the Great noticed that villages growing potatoes survived better. The crop grows underground, looks dirty and unimpressive, and peasants left it in the soil and dug it up as needed, so armies didn't bother taking it. As king, he pushed potato cultivation, which sometimes shaped the outcomes of his later wars. Peasants ignored his royal order to grow the suspect nightshade. In a story Ajay says may be apocryphal, Frederick then planted potatoes in heavily guarded royal gardens and told the soldiers to look away when people came to steal them.
stories.insight: A crop that is humble and hard to see can be a defence against plunder. And making something look forbidden can be a stronger incentive than ordering people to do it.
stories.quote: So this is the best way to make something work. It is to announce that it is illegal.

stories.topic: The Invasion of the Cavendish Banana
stories.summary: Retelling Vikram Doctor: India, with hundreds of banana varieties, gave bananas to the world. In Latin America they were reduced to one dominant strain, the yellow Cavendish, which Amit calls dull and tasteless. It won on economies of scale and shelf life. Now it has been sent back to India, and Doc laments that indigenous bananas are dying out. Pushpesh Pant makes the same complaint about weddings, where every buffet has a Punjabi stall and a chowmein stall. Yet Amit says he no longer worries. Homogenisation comes with the first burst of markets, but deeper markets and technology now support a long tail, as Stage.in shows for Haryanvi and Bhojpuri.
stories.insight: Scale first flattens diversity. Mature markets and cheap technology can later make room for variety again.
stories.quote: And this to me has become like a metaphor for the dangers of homogenization.

stories.topic: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan on a Vegetarian Diet
stories.summary: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan was invited to stay with vegetarian hosts for two or three days before performing, and they served him only vegetarian food. When he finally sang, he was a shadow of himself. The host asked how a man whose riyaz by the sea was said to drown out the roar of the waves could perform like this. His terse reply pinned it on the food, and Amit says he completely shares the maestro's desire for meat. Amit then turns to Ajay, who quotes George Bernard Shaw's Caesar on the barbarian who mistakes his tribe's customs for the law of nature.
stories.insight: It is a warning against ethnocentrism: imposing your own customs on others as if they were universal, and taking too much pride in what you think of as 'ours'.

stories.topic: Semolina Upma Was a Wartime Compromise
stories.summary: Krish Ashok's theory: one of several reasons more women worked and more girls went to school in South India is that the South ate rice. Rice is cooked in one batch, while rotis demand hours of labour every day. During a rice shortage (Amit thinks around WWII and the Japanese invasion of Burma), orders came from above telling the South to eat more wheat, backed by promotion campaigns. Women who didn't want to spend all day making rotis found a compromise, a form of wheat that cooks like rice: semolina. That gave us upma.
stories.insight: Dishes we call traditional often come out of a shock, here war, supply shortages and women's time. Food choices are bound up with gender and labour economics.
stories.quote: So they came up with a compromise, which was a kind of wheat that can be cooked like rice, semolina. And that is the origin of Semolina Upma.

stories.summary: An insight from Vikram Doctor: the main cooking fuel in old India was cow dung, which gives a low, slow flame. So Indian cooking was built around boiling. Tandoors and frying arrived with the Mughals, and fried food in India is relatively recent. Amit adds that this fuel role is another reason the cow is venerated.
stories.insight: Something as mundane as fuel can shape a whole cuisine. Even religious reverence can rest on material circumstances.
stories.quote: So again, just how something as simple as what is your fuel source can shape an entire cuisine.

stories.topic: Why Bombay Restaurants Were Bad (and FM Radio Too)
stories.summary: Five years earlier, Vikram Doctor told Amit that Bombay restaurants were bad because rents were so high that nobody could risk a niche or experimental menu. Everyone played safe with Udupi joints and paneer butter masala. Amit saw the same logic in Indian FM radio. Licences cost hundreds of crores and political news wasn't allowed, so stations had to play Bollywood to the lowest common denominator. No station would have aired The Seen and the Unseen or an economist chatting with an essayist. Podcasting changed that.
stories.insight: High fixed costs push producers toward the median taste. When entry gets cheaper, the experimental and the niche can survive.
stories.quote: So when you invest so much in opening a restaurant, you cannot experiment with a niche or with something experimental. You have to play to the lowest common denominator.

stories.topic: His Mother's Osaman Isn't on the Internet
stories.summary: Ajay is half Kutchi and half Kathiawari, and notes that many Gujaratis wouldn't understand an authentic Kathiawari conversation. A small subset of Kutchis make a dal called Osaman. He has searched the whole internet for his mother's version and cannot find it. He and his sister plan to film her making it, and he asks producer Vartika on air to help. Some of the physical motions she makes while cooking can't be described in words.
stories.insight: Recipes that live only in someone's hands vanish unless captured. Ajay frames this as preservation, not nostalgia: save the knowledge, then keep innovating with it.
stories.quote: I have searched the entire internet for the Osaman made by my mother, and it isn't there. It isn't there. I consider it one of the world's great dals and it's missing.

stories.topic: Vinay Singhal Had to Learn Two Languages
stories.summary: Vinay Singhal grew up speaking Haryanvi in a Haryana village. When he moved to a town school in ninth standard, he had to learn English from scratch. When he moved to a big city, he had to learn Hindi. Today Stage, his platform for Haryanvi and other dialects, is reversing that pressure. Kids come to him with tears in their eyes saying they no longer feel ashamed of their language.
stories.insight: Hindi has steamrolled dialects like Haryanvi, Maithili and Bhojpuri. Long-tail technology can restore dignity to them, not just preserve them.
stories.quote: For the first time in my life, I don't have to feel ashamed of my language.

stories.topic: The Tagore Estate's Fly in Amber
stories.summary: Rajeswari Sengupta told Ajay that after Rabindranath Tagore's death, the heirs who controlled his intellectual property policed it strictly. They demanded that his works be performed exactly as they were in his time. Ajay calls this a tragedy. He adds that although he's no friend of rap, surely there should be a Rabindra rap sangeet. Amit replies there surely is, and points out that Shakespeare, never wrapped in cotton wool, has been reworked by everyone from David Gilmour to the rapper Akala.
stories.insight: Freezing a creator's work cuts it off from the recombination that keeps culture alive. Reverence that forbids reinterpretation slowly kills the thing it reveres.
stories.quote: It is a certain sad view of the world where something is pristine and pure and you just want to hang on to it for the rest of eternity

recommendations.item: How The Desperate Norwegian Salmon Industry Created A Sushi Staple
recommendations.creator: Jess Jiang
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for the salmon sushi story that opens the episode.
recommendations.reason: The full account of how Norway's salmon glut turned into the world's default sushi.

recommendations.item: The Indianness of Indian Food (Episode 95 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Doctor
recommendations.context: Amit's main source for the Cavendish banana, cow dung fuel, marigolds from Mexico, idlis and Bombay restaurant stories.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Vikram Doctor the world's best food writer and describes the episode as tremendous.

recommendations.item: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pushpesh Pant
recommendations.context: Cited for Pant's rant about Punjabi-plus-chowmein wedding buffets and his pet peeves.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls the episode remarkable. Pant has decades of experience and urges Indians to explore their own country's food diversity.

recommendations.item: We Are All Amits From Africa (Episode 343 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok and Naren Shenoy
recommendations.context: Source of the upma origin story and the discussion of how caste and class shape cuisine.
recommendations.reason: Covers how circumstances such as rice shortages and caste lines produce distinct foods.

recommendations.item: A Scientist in the Kitchen (Episode 204 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok
recommendations.context: Mentioned as Amit's earlier episode with Krish Ashok, among his episodes on Indian food.
recommendations.reason: Another of Amit's conversations on where Indian food comes from.

recommendations.item: India: Cookbook
recommendations.creator: Pushpesh Pant
recommendations.context: Amit reads from it about Vasco da Gama's cargo: 1,500 tons of pepper, 28 tons of ginger, 8 tons of cinnamon and 7 tons of cloves.
recommendations.reason: Calls it a great book. It shows that food moved both ways: traders brought leavened bread, baking and noodles, and India gave Europe curry, mangoes and chutney.

recommendations.item: Cooking the world's oldest known curry
recommendations.creator: Soity Banerjee
recommendations.context: Written by a former editor of Amit's Hindu Business Line column, who tried to recreate an Indus Valley meal.
recommendations.reason: As Amit recalls it, the only ingredient we would recognise today is baingan, which shows how little of our food is native.

recommendations.item: The Columbian Exchange
recommendations.creator: Wikipedia
recommendations.context: Amit's explanation of how potato, mirchi, tomato and amrood reached India from the Americas.
recommendations.reason: The background to why so much of 'Indian' food is actually from the Americas.

recommendations.item: Did Frederick The Great Introduce The Potato To Germany?
recommendations.creator: Matt Robinson
recommendations.context: Linked alongside Ajay's story about Frederick the Great, potatoes and the guarded royal gardens.
recommendations.reason: Lets you dig into a story Ajay himself flags as possibly apocryphal.

recommendations.item: Against the Grain
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: After Ajay used Scott's argument about grain and early states, Amit urged all viewers to read it.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a magnificent book and a masterpiece that everyone should read, along with every other book Scott has written.

recommendations.item: Caesar and Cleopatra
recommendations.creator: George Bernard Shaw
recommendations.context: Ajay quotes Shaw's Caesar after the Bade Ghulam Ali Khan story.
recommendations.reason: Source of the line about the barbarian who mistakes his tribe's customs for the law of nature. It sums up the episode's case against ethnocentrism.

recommendations.item: Stage.in
recommendations.creator: Vinay Singhal
recommendations.context: Amit describes it as a 'Netflix for Bharat' with content in Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and other dialects.
recommendations.reason: Evidence that technology and long-tail markets can reverse the homogenisation of dialects.

recommendations.item: When and where do great feats of architecture come about?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's own blog post, cited while comparing architecture to food.
recommendations.reason: Argues that grand structures are a power move to make peasants bow, and that more totalitarian regimes build more imposing ones. Good architecture comes from local conditions.

recommendations.item: Make Me a Canteen for My Soul (Episode 304 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Sameer Seth and Yash Bhanage
recommendations.context: With the founders of Bombay Canteen and O Pedro, which Amit calls the best restaurant in Bombay.
recommendations.reason: About preserving food heritage through memories and stories. Amit recalls Bombay Canteen asking people to send in their grandmothers' recipes and serving them as a day's menu.

recommendations.item: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Episode 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Singhal
recommendations.context: Source of the story of a Haryanvi speaker forced to learn English and then Hindi.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Singhal a good guy and a great entrepreneur. His story shows Hindi's pressure on dialects and how Stage is reversing it.

recommendations.item: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Naren Shenoy
recommendations.context: Linked alongside Naren's observation that Brahmins and Dalits in the same village eat very different food.
recommendations.reason: More from the friend Amit plans to research the caste and class roots of cuisine with.

recommendations.item: Early Indians
recommendations.creator: Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: The first of Amit's three book recommendations for the episode.
recommendations.reason: Uses genes of living people to reconstruct thousands of years of history, which Amit finds mind-blowing. It traces how we came from Africa, the migrations into India, and how caste endogamy set in about 2,000 years ago. Amit says it contains fundamental truths.

recommendations.item: Early Indians (Episode 112 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with the author.
recommendations.reason: Source of his realisation that India's migrant groups mixed for thousands of years before endogamy locked in.

recommendations.item: Who We Are and How We Got Here
recommendations.creator: David Reich
recommendations.context: Cited while discussing caste endogamy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the contrast between the Han Chinese as one large population and India as thousands of small ones.

recommendations.item: Alice Evans Studies the Great Gender Divergence (Episode 297 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Alice Evans
recommendations.context: Mentioned while explaining how caste endogamy affects women's lives.
recommendations.reason: Explores how maintaining endogamy requires controlling female sexuality, which drives female seclusion.

recommendations.item: Mayabono Biharini (from BEDROOM)
recommendations.creator: Somlata
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes after Ajay said there should be a Rabindra rap sangeet and Amit said there surely is.
recommendations.reason: Rabindrasangeet breaking out of genre boundaries: Tagore's music doing what living culture should.

recommendations.item: Sonnet 18
recommendations.creator: William Shakespeare
recommendations.context: Amit's counterexample to the Tagore estate.
recommendations.reason: Shakespeare was never wrapped in cotton wool, so everyone has reworked him, which is how culture should work.

recommendations.item: Sonnet 18 (David Gilmour performance)
recommendations.creator: David Gilmour
recommendations.context: Amit mentions the Pink Floyd guitarist performing Shakespeare's sonnet.
recommendations.reason: An example of a classic being freely remixed across eras and genres.

recommendations.item: Sonnet 18 (Akala performance)
recommendations.creator: Akala
recommendations.context: A rap rendition of Sonnet 18 at about the five-minute mark of the linked video.
recommendations.reason: Shows Shakespeare turned into hip hop. Amit says culture is a party: mix karo, dance karo, enjoy karo.

recommendations.item: Monkey Cuisine
recommendations.creator: BBC Earth
recommendations.context: Linked for Ajay's story of the Japanese monkeys who learned to wash sandy rice in seawater.
recommendations.reason: Documents non-human culture: an idea, not instinct, spreading from one female to her band and then to other bands.

recommendations.item: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants
recommendations.creator: Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: The second of Amit's three linked book recommendations; he pressed it on Varun Grover.
recommendations.reason: Reads India's past through living languages. Migrating men married local women, so a boy spoke his mother's tongue as a toddler and switched to the men's language later. Amit also cites its insights on the origins of Hindustani and Urdu and why Ghalib sometimes wrote obscurely. A must-read if you love language or India.

recommendations.item: India Moving
recommendations.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
recommendations.context: The third book, a history of internal migration in India over 2,000 years that zooms in where Tony Joseph zooms out.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it one of the great books of the last ten years, though not much written about. Its big insight is that marriage is India's largest source of internal migration.

recommendations.item: Understanding India Through Its Languages (Episode 232 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Peggy Mohan.
recommendations.reason: A conversation companion to Wanderers, Kings, Merchants.

recommendations.item: India = Migration (Episode 128 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chinmay Tumbe
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Chinmay Tumbe.
recommendations.reason: A conversation companion to India Moving.

recommendations.item: Varun Grover Is in the House (Episode 292 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Varun Grover
recommendations.context: Varun Grover recorded with Amit right after Peggy Mohan, and Amit gave him her book.
recommendations.reason: Linked through that anecdote: Amit was flabbergasted that Grover hadn't read it.

recommendations.item: Whole-grain sourdough bread
recommendations.context: Ajay's first recommendation, a practice rather than a book.
recommendations.reason: He calls it Pareto superior to industrial yeast bread on taste and especially on health. It's fun to make, though you have to work to keep it near 20°C in India.

recommendations.item: Kefir grain (Kefirwala)
recommendations.context: Ajay's second recommendation: kefir, a fermented milk. He got a high-quality batch of grains from Bangalore.
recommendations.reason: Good for your health and fun to explore, even though its ideal 20°C fermentation temperature is hard to get in India.

core_ideas.concept: Nothing Is Indian, Everything Is Indian
core_ideas.explanation: Almost nothing we think of as quintessentially Indian started here: stitched clothes, the Patiala salwar, potatoes, chillies, tomatoes, guava, marigolds, saffron, possibly idli fermentation, rajma chawal, tandoori chicken, even English. That is not a loss. Once influences arrive and are absorbed, they become ours.
core_ideas.quote: and therefore you can make the narrow argument that nothing is really Indian so we shouldn't call anything Indian per se. But my broader argument would be that everything is Indian.

core_ideas.explanation: Food, language and clothes are best as mixtures. English borrows from Latin, Greek, Persian, Anglo-Saxon and Hindustani ('juggernaut' comes from Jagannath). So English is an Indian language, and arguably not even purely an English one. Purity is a myth; mixing is the joy.
core_ideas.quote: But the best things are always a khichdi, a delightful mixture

core_ideas.concept: Food Has Always Flowed Both Ways
core_ideas.explanation: The Columbian Exchange brought New World crops such as potato, mirchi, tomato and amrood to India. The spice trade drew Europeans here, and trade flowed in both directions. Indian cuisine as we know it is a product of global exchange.
core_ideas.quote: the traders brought with them the culinary secrets of leavened bread, baking, and noodles. In return, the Indians introduced the Europeans to the joys of curry, mangoes and chutney.

core_ideas.explanation: From James C. Scott: grain is calorie-dense, storable, transportable and easy to seize, which made early states and marauding armies possible. Banana and papaya don't keep, so there is little to grab. The potato, growing out of sight underground, was a survival crop that armies overlooked.
core_ideas.quote: Grain is a new milestone in human history that it can be grabbed, it can be stored, and it is dense in calories. So grain is very dangerous.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's two-stage model: a cuisine starts from local conditions such as produce, climate, fuel, class and caste, then mixes with global influences shaped by mimetic desire. Examples from the episode: US PL 480 wheat bringing rotis south; wartime rice shortages producing upma; a nawab's bad teeth producing the galouti kebab (by legend); Travancore's king promoting kappa (tapioca) during a 19th-century rice shortage; cow dung fuel making Indian food boiled rather than fried; Bombay rents killing experimental restaurants; caste separating Brahmin and Dalit kitchens in the same village.
core_ideas.quote: So you start with a local base and then this khichdi comes in and that's also contingent, what comes in from where, what influences take over

core_ideas.concept: Mass Media Homogenises, the Internet Diversifies
core_ideas.explanation: Radio, TV and film flattened diversity. America converged on one standard accent, and state promotion of Hindi replaced the varied, bottom-up Hindustani of 75 years ago. Ajay notes that Mussolini was the first to abuse radio on a large scale. The internet reverses this: YouTube, Stage and podcasts let Konkani (really many Konkanis), Haryanvi, regional cooking and niche talk shows survive.
core_ideas.quote: Stage one of electronics is the homogenization of radio and TV, which is mass media. But now we've reached that new world of the internet where people can go to YouTube and discover Konkani shows.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that if culture is a melding of influences, nobody can 'own' it. The Tagore estate's rules show what policing culture costs, and Shakespeare rapped by Akala shows what freedom gains.
core_ideas.quote: If it's cultural, how can there be appropriation? Culture is about the melding of influences

core_ideas.concept: Preserve Without Freezing: No Fly in Amber
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's balance: capture inherited knowledge, like his mother's Osaman, while it still exists. But don't glorify the past or turn culture into a museum piece. Food, language and architecture should keep evolving with local conditions, new technology and creativity, without simply copying others.
core_ideas.quote: So it is a plea for preservation. At the same time it's not a conservative's plea for stagnation. It's not a fly in the amber.

core_ideas.concept: Grand Architecture Is a Power Play
core_ideas.explanation: Imposing buildings are usually built by the powerful to make people bow and to show off borrowed prestige. Thought through from first principles, architecture should fit local weather, materials and craftsmanship. Ajay argues food culture should be judged the same way.
core_ideas.quote: The more totalitarian the regime, the greater their interest in imposing structures.

core_ideas.explanation: Waves of migrants mixed freely for a couple of thousand years. Then, around 2,000 years ago, an ideology from the Gangetic belt won out and enforced caste endogamy. That required controlling women, which drove female seclusion. It also split India into thousands of small populations with separate cuisines. Ajay compares these to island ecosystems evolving in isolation.
core_ideas.quote: David Reich says that if you want to look for a large population, the Han Chinese are a large population. India is full of many different thousands of small populations.

core_ideas.explanation: From Chinmay Tumbe: the largest source of internal migration in India is women moving at marriage. Outside elite circles, these women leave their whole lives and friendships behind and start over. Men often keep the same friends all their lives.
core_ideas.quote: the largest source of internal migration in India is marriage.

core_ideas.explanation: Culture means all learned behaviour: language, customs, law, science, problem-solving. It sits on top of our biological hardware. Animals have it too: a Japanese monkey's rice-washing trick spread from band to band. Because culture is software, we can question and rewrite it. The obstacle is ethnocentrism, judging the world from your own tribe's point of view, which Ajay says is widely prevalent in India.
core_ideas.quote: everything that is the software about Homo sapiens is culture.

core_ideas.concept: Health Depends on the Food System
core_ideas.explanation: Homogenisation is often driven by big industrial food companies that want standardisation; McDonald's fries everywhere use a single Idaho Russet potato. Questioning processed food is self-preservation. The cultural case and the health case agree: more artisanal, local food would mean a new cuisine every 50 to 100 km.
core_ideas.quote: It is impossible to think deeply about the health system without thinking deeply about the food system.

core_ideas.explanation: Dahi ferments best at about 36°C, which suits India. Sourdough and kefir need about 20°C, which rarely happens here. All bread was once sourdough, until industrial yeast took over. India's climate is why it developed mainly unleavened breads like roti and naan, with khamiri roti in the cooler north as the exception.
core_ideas.quote: So in India we came to the culture of unfermented breads, the roti and the naan and so on.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit sneaks in proof that English is Indian: the word juggernaut comes from Jagannath, 'and indeed the show, one could argue, is like a juggernaut blazing its way through the forests of YouTube.'

Amit imagines Norway's salmon glut spilling into the streets: classrooms so full of salmon that kids couldn't go to school, police stations so full that law and order broke down. He calls it a 'salmon maximizer', like the famous paperclip maximizer thought experiment.

Ajay tells half-Bengali Amit that some say the rasgulla's geographical indicator belongs to Odisha and that the idea was brought by the Portuguese. Amit: 'Sugar is poison, colonialism is bad, now we know why. Carry on.'

Ajay's punchline to Frederick the Great's guarded potato gardens: 'This is the best way to make something work. It is to announce that it is illegal. So now you know why cryptocurrency has such a great future in India.'
Amit on bananas: 'in the best way possible, we are a banana republic.' The bananas we gave the world went, 'in the worst way possible', to the banana republics of Latin America.
Amit savours the 'Pushpesh Pant pet peeves': the tyranny of the tandoor, the curse of the curry and the myth of Mughlai. 'And if he wore Patiala pants like me, two more Ps.'
Ajay swears off basmati rice, calling it a tyranny. Amit, alliterating in Pushpesh Pant's honour, upgrades it to 'the barbarism of basmati', and Ajay to 'the brutality of basmati'.
How to measure someone's distance from a Maharashtrian village: say 'wangi' and you're close; 'baingan' is one step removed; then brinjal, aubergine, and, furthest of all, the American 'eggplant'.
As Ajay explains Kutchi pride, Amit butts in: 'If Kutchis invented the underwear, the kachha, which is so impressive to me, but carry on.'
Bombay restaurants all serving paneer butter masala reminds Amit of Pratap Bhanu Mehta, 'because he's called PBM'.

Ajay: 'I'm no friend of rap music, but surely there should be a Rabindra rap sangeet.' Amit admits that as a kid he thought rap was noise ('People are talking, why can't they sing?') but now loves it, and declares culture a party: 'mix karo, dance karo, enjoy karo.'
Amit's definition of culture, which he says they should rename the show after: 'Everything is everything.'
Amit's sign-off after Ajay's sourdough and kefir sermon: 'May you have peace in your life, but ferment in your food.'
George Bernard Shaw's Caesar and Cleopatra, quoted by Ajay: 'He is a barbarian who thinks that the customs of his tribe and island are the law of nature.'
Ajay uses the quip 'a language is a dialect with a navy' to argue that pre-Independence Hindustani was really many dialects, flattened later into standard Hindi.
Ajay notes that radio was first abused on a large scale by Mussolini, the start of mass media's homogenising era.
Monsoon Wedding: Amit recalls a character constantly eating marigolds, the 'Indian' wedding flower that actually came from Mexico.
The Japanese monkeys who learned to wash sandy rice in seawater, cited by Ajay as documented proof that non-human animals have culture.
The galouti kebab legend: a nawab with bad teeth needed meat that melted in the mouth, and a classic dish was born.
